danish.title: Fjerde bog (1806) — Kapitel 7
paragraphs: Der var gået to måneder, siden nyheden om slaget ved Austerlitz og tabet af fyrst Andrej var nået til Lyse Bjerge (Bald Hills), og trods breve sendt gennem ambassaden og alle eftersøgninger var hans lig ikke fundet, og han var heller ikke på listen over fanger. Det værste for hans pårørende var, at der stadig var en mulighed for, at han var blevet samlet op på slagmarken af egnens beboere, og at han nu lå et sted, helbredende eller døende, alene blandt fremmede og ude af stand til at sende besked. De aviser, hvorfra den gamle fyrste først erfarede om nederlaget ved Austerlitz, meddelte som sædvanlig meget kortfattet og vagt, at russerne efter strålende kampe havde måttet trække sig tilbage i fuldkommen orden. Den gamle fyrste forstod af denne officielle rapport, at vores hær var blevet besejret. En uge efter avisens beretning om slaget kom et brev fra Kutuzov, der meddelte fyrsten, hvilken skæbne hans søn havde lidt.

»Deres søn,« skrev Kutuzov, »faldt for mine øjne med en fane i hånden og i spidsen for et regiment — han faldt som en helt, værdig sin far og sit fædreland. Til min og hele hærens store sorg er det stadig uvist, om han er i live eller ej. Jeg trøster mig selv og Dem med håbet om, at Deres søn lever, for ellers ville han være nævnt blandt de officerer, der er fundet på slagmarken, en liste, som er blevet sendt mig under hvidt flag.«

Da den gamle fyrste modtog denne nyhed sent om aftenen, da han var alene i sit arbejdsværelse, gik han næste morgen sin sædvanlige tur, men var tavs over for sin forvalter, gartneren og arkitekten, og skønt han så meget grimmig ud, sagde han ikke et ord til nogen.
Da fyrstinde Marja kom ind til ham på det sædvanlige tidspunkt, stod han ved sin drejebænk og så som sædvanlig ikke op.

»Ah, fyrstinde Marja!« sagde han pludselig med unaturlig stemme og kastede sin mejsel fra sig. (Hjulet fortsatte med at dreje af sin egen kraft, og fyrstinde Marja huskede længe den døende knirken af det hjul, der smeltede sammen i hendes erindring med det, der fulgte.)

Hun gik hen til ham, så hans ansigt, og noget brast inden i hende. Hendes øjne dæmredes. Ved udtrykket i faderens ansigt — ikke sørgende, ikke knust, men vredt og anspændt — forstod hun, at der hang en forfærdelig ulykke over hende, klar til at knuse hende, den værste i livet, en hun endnu ikke havde oplevet, ubodelig og ufattelig — døden af en, hun elskede.
»Far! Andrej!« — sagde den usikre, klodsede fyrstinde med en så ubeskrivelig charme af sorg og selvforglemmelse, at hendes far ikke kunne bære hendes blik, men vendte sig bort med et hulk.
»Dårlige nyheder! Han er ikke blandt fangerne og ikke blandt de faldne! Kutuzov skriver ...« og han skreg så gennemtrængende, som om han med det skrig ville jage fyrstinden bort ... »Dræbt!«

Fyrstinden faldt ikke om og besvimede ikke. Hun var allerede bleg, men da hun hørte de ord, forandredes hendes ansigt, og noget lyste op i hendes smukke, strålende øjne. Det var, som om en glæde — en ophøjet glæde hinsides denne verdens glæder og sorger — overskyllede den store sorg i hende. Hun glemte al frygt for sin far, gik hen til ham, tog hans hånd, og idet hun trak ham ned, lagde sin arm om hans tynde, senede hals.
»Far,« sagde hun, »vend dig ikke bort fra mig, lad os græde sammen.«
»Slyngler! Skurke!« skreg den gamle mand og vendte ansigtet bort fra hende. »Ødelægger hæren, ødelægger menneskerne! Og hvorfor? Gå, gå og fortæl det til Lise.«

Fyrstinden sank hjælpeløst sammen i en lænestol ved siden af sin far og græd. Hun så sin bror, som da han tog afsked med hende og Lise (hans kone) — hans blik ømt, men dog stolt. Hun så ham øm og adspredt, da han satte det lille ikon på. »Troede han? Havde han angret sin vantro? Var han nu dér? Dér i det evige fredens og salighedens rige?« tænkte hun.
»Far, fortæl mig, hvordan det skete,« sagde hun gennem sine tårer.
»Gå! Gå! Faldne i kamp, hvor Ruslands bedste mænd og Ruslands ære blev ført i fordærv. Gå, fyrstinde Marja. Gå og fortæl det til Lise. Jeg kommer bagefter.«

Da fyrstinde Marja vendte tilbage fra sin far, sad den lille fyrstinde og arbejdede med sit håndarbejde og så op med det ejendommelige udtryk af indre, lykkelig ro, der er ejendommeligt for gravide kvinder. Det var tydeligt, at hendes øjne ikke så fyrstinde Marja, men kiggede indad ... ind i sig selv ... på noget glædeligt og hemmeligt, der udfoldede sig i hende.
»Marja,« sagde hun og rykkede sig fra broderrammen, idet hun lænede sig tilbage, »giv mig din hånd.« Hun tog sin svigerindes hånd og holdt den under sin mave.
Hendes øjne smilede forventningsfuldt, hendes dunede lille overslæbe løftede sig og forblev løftet i barnlig lykke.
Fyrstinde Marja knælede foran hende og skjulte ansigtet i folderne af sin svigerindes kjole.
»Der, dér! Kan du mærke det? Jeg har det så underligt. Og ved du hvad, Marja, jeg vil komme til at elske ham så højt,« sagde Lise og så med lyse, lykkelige øjne på sin svigerinde.
Fyrstinde Marja kunne ikke løfte hovedet — hun græd.
»Hvad er der i vejen, Marja?«
»Ingenting ... jeg er bare ked af det ... ked af det for Andrejs skyld,« sagde hun og tørrede sine tårer af mod sin svigerindes knæ.

Flere gange i løbet af formiddagen forsøgte fyrstinde Marja at forberede sin svigerinde, og hver gang begyndte hun at græde. Så uopmærksom den lille fyrstinde end var, rørte disse tårer, hvis årsag hun ikke forstod, hende. Hun sagde ingenting, men så sig uroligt om, som om hun ledte efter noget. Inden middag kom den gamle fyrste, som hun altid var bange for, ind i hendes værelse med et ejendommeligt rastløst og ondskabsfuldt udtryk og gik ud igen uden et ord. Hun så på fyrstinde Marja, sad så et stykke tid og tænkte med det udtryk af opmærksom indadvendthed, der kun ses hos gravide kvinder, og brast pludselig i gråd.
»Er der kommet noget fra Andrej?« spurgte hun.
»Nej, du ved, det er for tidligt til nyheder. Men min far er urolig, og jeg er bange.«
»Så der er ingenting?«
»Ingenting,« svarede fyrstinde Marja og så fast på sin svigerinde med sine strålende øjne.

Hun havde besluttet ikke at fortælle hende det og overtalte sin far til at skjule den forfærdelige nyhed for hende, indtil efter fødslen, der ventedes om få dage. Fyrstinde Marja og den gamle fyrste bar og skjulte hver sin sorg på deres egen måde. Den gamle fyrste ville ikke nære noget håb: han havde besluttet, at fyrst Andrej var dræbt, og skønt han sendte en embedsmand til Østrig for at søge efter spor af sin søn, bestilte han et monument fra Moskva, som han agtede at rejse i sin egen have til hans minde, og han fortalte alle, at hans søn var faldet. Han forsøgte ikke at ændre sin hidtidige levevis, men kræfterne svigtede ham. Han gik mindre, spiste mindre, sov mindre og blev svagere for hver dag. Fyrstinde Marja håbede. Hun bad for sin bror som levende og ventede stadig på nyheden om hans hjemkomst.

english.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Two months had passed since news of the Battle of Austerlitz and the loss of Prince Andrew had reached Bald Hills. Despite letters sent through the embassy and extensive searches, his body had not been found, nor was he on any list of prisoners. Worst of all for his family was the lingering possibility that he had been picked up on the battlefield by local people and might now be lying somewhere, recovering or dying, alone among strangers, unable to send word. The official newspapers, from which the old prince first learned of the defeat at Austerlitz, reported — as usual very briefly and vaguely — that after brilliant engagements the Russians had been forced to retreat and had done so in perfect order. The old prince understood from this report that the army had been defeated. A week after the newspaper account of the battle, a letter arrived from Kutuzov informing the prince of what had befallen his son.

"Your son," Kutuzov wrote, "fell before my eyes, a standard in his hand, at the head of a regiment — he fell as a hero, worthy of his father and his fatherland. To my great regret and that of the whole army, it is still uncertain whether he is alive or not. I take comfort, and offer it to you, in the hope that your son is alive, since otherwise he would have been listed among the officers found on the battlefield — a list which has been sent to me under a flag of truce."

After receiving this news late in the evening, when he was alone in his study, the old prince went for his walk as usual the next morning. But he was silent with his steward, the gardener, and the architect, and though he looked very stern, he said nothing to anyone.
When Princess Mary came to him at the usual hour, he was working at his lathe and, as always, didn't look up when she entered.

"Ah, Princess Mary!" he suddenly said in an unnatural voice, throwing down his chisel. The wheel continued spinning by its own momentum, and Princess Mary would always remember the dying creak of that wheel, which merged in her memory with everything that followed.

She went up to him, saw his face, and something broke inside her. Her eyes grew dim. From the expression on her father's face — not sad, not broken, but angry and working unnaturally — she could see that some terrible catastrophe was hanging over her and about to crush her. The worst thing in life, something she had never experienced — irreparable and incomprehensible — the death of someone she loved.
"Father! Andrew!" said the plain, awkward princess with such indescribable beauty of grief and selflessness that her father couldn't bear her look and turned away with a sob.
"Bad news! He's not among the prisoners or the dead! Kutuzov writes..." and he let out a piercing scream, as if trying to drive the princess away with it. "Killed!"

The princess didn't collapse or faint. She was already pale, but when she heard these words, her face changed and something lit up in her beautiful, radiant eyes. It was as if a supreme joy — a joy beyond the joys and sorrows of this world — flooded over the immense grief within her. She forgot all fear of her father, went up to him, took his hand, and drawing him down, put her arm around his thin, bony neck.
"Father," she said, "don't turn away from me. Let us cry together."
"Scoundrels! Villains!" the old man shrieked, turning his face away from her. "Destroying the army, destroying men! And for what? Go — go and tell Lise."

The princess sank helplessly into an armchair beside her father and wept. She saw her brother as he had been at the moment he said goodbye to her and to Lise — his expression tender yet proud. She saw him tender and amused as he had been when he put on the little icon. "Did he believe? Had he repented of his doubt? Was he there now? There, in the realm of eternal peace and blessedness?" she wondered.
"Father, tell me how it happened," she asked through her tears.
"Go! Go! Killed in battle, where the finest Russian men and Russia's glory were led to destruction. Go, Princess Mary. Go and tell Lise. I'll follow."

When Princess Mary returned from her father, the little princess sat doing needlework, looking up with that curious expression of inner, happy calm that is unique to pregnant women. It was clear that her eyes didn't see Princess Mary — they were looking inward, into herself, at something joyful and mysterious happening within her.
"Mary," she said, pushing away from the embroidery frame and leaning back, "give me your hand." She took her sister-in-law's hand and placed it below her waist.
Her eyes smiled with anticipation; her soft, downy lip lifted and stayed raised in childlike happiness.
Princess Mary knelt before her and buried her face in the folds of her sister-in-law's dress.
"There — there! Do you feel it? It's such a strange feeling. And you know, Mary, I'm going to love him so much," said Lise, gazing at her sister-in-law with bright, happy eyes.
Princess Mary couldn't lift her head. She was crying.
"What's the matter, Mary?"
"Nothing... it's just that I feel sad... sad about Andrew," she said, wiping her tears on her sister-in-law's knee.

Several times that morning Princess Mary tried to prepare her sister-in-law for the news, but each time she started, she began to cry. Unobservant as the little princess was, these tears, whose cause she didn't understand, unsettled her. She said nothing but glanced around uneasily, as if searching for something. Before dinner the old prince, of whom she was always afraid, came into her room with a particularly restless and hostile expression, then left again without a word. She looked at Princess Mary, then sat thinking for a while with that look of inward attention seen only in pregnant women, and suddenly began to cry.
"Has there been any word from Andrew?" she asked.
"No — you know it's too soon for news. But Father is worried, and I'm frightened."
"So there's nothing?"
"Nothing," answered Princess Mary, looking firmly at her sister-in-law with her radiant eyes.

She had resolved not to tell her and had persuaded her father to hide the terrible news until after the birth, which was expected any day. Princess Mary and the old prince each bore and concealed their grief in their own way. The old prince refused to hold out any hope. He made up his mind that Prince Andrew had been killed, and although he sent an official to Austria to search for traces of his son, he ordered a monument from Moscow that he planned to erect in his own garden as a memorial, and he told everyone that his son had been killed. He tried not to change his usual routine, but his strength was failing. He walked less, ate less, slept less, and grew weaker every day. Princess Mary held onto hope. She prayed for her brother as for a living man and was constantly waiting for news of his return.
